summary: This informational RFC explains why a single solution was chosen for MPLS Transport Profile OAM, and gives the reasons for selecting one rather than supporting several competing approaches.

plainLanguage.summary: When two groups suggest different tools for the same job, picking only one avoids confusion. This explains why.

questions: why one oam solution for mpls-tp
what is the cost of multiple oam solutions
how do networks handle two incompatible protocols
subtitle: Why MPLS-TP standardized a single OAM solution instead of supporting multiple competing approaches.

tldr.problem: During MPLS-TP development, multiple groups proposed different OAM solutions for transport networks, raising the question of whether to standardize one solution or many.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC argues against standardizing multiple solutions by examining the technical, operational, and economic costs of coexistence, interworking, and migration when incompatible protocols must work together.
tldr.outcome: The IETF selected a single coherent OAM solution for MPLS-TP based on extending existing MPLS tools, avoiding the complexity and expense that would arise from supporting multiple incompatible approaches.

today: RFC 6670 is an Informational RFC that documents the standardization decision to use a single OAM solution for MPLS-TP. The chosen solution (documented in related RFCs) remains the standard approach for MPLS transport networks.

sections.title: Background
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) extends MPLS technology for use in carrier transport networks, which require operations and maintenance tools at the level of traditional transport networks like SONET/SDH. During development, a Joint Working Team (JWT) of ITU-T and IETF experts concluded that MPLS could be extended to meet these requirements. However, during standardization, multiple proposals emerged for OAM solutions.

This document explains the IETF's decision to define and publish a single, coherent OAM solution rather than standardize competing alternatives. The analysis examines what would happen if two incompatible MPLS-TP OAM protocols coexisted: the costs to vendors, operators, and end users; the complexity of interworking; and the challenges of migration when protocols need to work together across networks.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS is being extended to work in carrier networks. Some groups wanted one design, others wanted a different one. This document explains why standardizing only one design is much cheaper and less messy than supporting two.

sections.title: Reasons Against Multiple OAM Solutions
sections.content:
MPLS-TP is an MPLS technology. It extends MPLS in compatible ways, reusing design philosophies and existing OAM tools. This means MPLS-TP OAM should align with MPLS OAM, not diverge from it.

MPLS-TP is a convergence technology. Communication networks are gradually collapsing multiple layers into a TCP/IP/MPLS stack. Service providers deployed MPLS OAM a decade ago and will continue using it. The question is not which OAM to invent, but whether to use one or two sets of OAM tools in the converged network.

OAM must work end-to-end. LSPs and pseudowires can cross network operator boundaries. Both ends of a path must understand a common OAM protocol. This is especially critical for equipment deployed globally by different operators, which could be interconnected anywhere.

Interworking is costly. If two protocols coexist, they must either be isolated into incompatible islands, universally deployed (more than doubling development and testing costs), or connected with interworking gateways (which add complexity, cost, and fragility, and introduce risks of translation errors).
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS already works, people use it, and paths need to work end-to-end. If two OAM tools exist, they either never touch (bad for networks), both must be in everything (expensive and buggy), or you need translators (slow and fragile).

sections.title: Complexity and Migration
sections.content:
Multiple solutions create operational burden. When multiple protocols are available, operators must decide which to deploy. Evaluating both protocols requires comparative testing, which doubles lab costs. Vendors face pressure to implement both, doubling development costs and increasing defect rates. The RFC notes that code complexity and defect rates increase more than linearly with code size, and testing for conflicts between two protocols adds further cost.

Migration between protocols is expensive. If an operator deploys one OAM solution and later needs to migrate to another (for example, after acquiring a competitor using different protocols), hardware components must be replaced in the field at significant cost. A rolling upgrade requires temporary dual-capability hardware, which is more complex and costly. During transition, the network operates in dual-mode, adding complexity and expense to operations.

All of these costs ultimately fall on end users. Standardizing one solution avoids these expenses entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: Vendors have to build both. Operators have to pick. Networks need to test both. If you pick wrong, you're stuck. All that costs money, and customers pay for it.

sections.title: Coexistence Models Don't Solve the Problem
sections.content:
The RFC examines several models for running two incompatible OAM protocols in the same network. In an integrated model, nodes support one protocol, another, or both (dual-mode), but none perform translation. This leads to suboptimal paths, network partitioning, and operational complexity. Fast reroute or misconnectivity can cause mismatched nodes to be interconnected, disrupting traffic and breaking diagnostics.

In an island model, regions of nodes using the same protocol are connected via tunnels (layering) or translation gateways at borders. Tunneling adds management complexity and debugging difficulty because intermediate hops are hidden. Translation gateways are costly, fragile, and unstable. When OAM functions must traverse multiple islands, translation happens repeatedly, risking information loss and errors (like the children's game "telephone").

Both models fail to solve the fundamental problem: MPLS networks need end-to-end OAM. Eventually, if two solutions coexist, they will meet, and neither coexistence model provides a clean or inexpensive solution.
sections.plainLanguage: You can try to keep the two protocols separate, but networks expand, merge, and get rerouted. Eventually they have to talk to each other, and then everything gets complicated.

sections.title: Arguments for Two Solutions and Their Rebuttal
sections.content:
Some argued for a second solution on the grounds that the IETF standardization was slow, that similarity to Ethernet OAM would be beneficial, that two deployment scenarios (Packet Switched Networks and Packet Transport Networks) existed, or that markets should decide. The RFC addresses each claim.

On speed: Opening discussions on a second solution increases workload and slows consensus, not accelerates it.

On Ethernet similarity: While similarity might simplify some implementations, the need for end-to-end consistency with MPLS OAM networks outweighs this benefit. Moreover, a second solution still requires gateways between MPLS-TP and other technologies, so it solves nothing. Implementation simplicity can equally be achieved by making MPLS-TP OAM similar to MPLS OAM, which aligns with the client technology (IP/MPLS).

On different scenarios: The claimed distinction between packet-switched and packet-transport networks was not formally documented; it was largely a circular argument justifying the second solution.

On market choice: Market choice works when protocols offer different features. When they offer the same function but are incompatible, choice becomes a burden, not a benefit.
sections.plainLanguage: Some groups thought a second design was better, faster, or simpler. But standardizing one design actually moves faster, and compatibility matters more than looking like Ethernet.
